title: Jägermeister Hangover: Why Jäger and Jägerbombs Hit So Hard
excerpt: Why Jägermeister hangovers feel so brutal: fast cold shots, sugar, herbal congeners, and the caffeine in Jägerbombs. Myths debunked, plus how to prevent and recover.
metaDescription: Why do Jägermeister hangovers hit so hard? Shots, sugar, herbal congeners and Jägerbomb caffeine explained, plus how to prevent and recover from one.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Jägermeister hangovers have a reputation for being brutal, and the reputation is mostly earned, but not because of anything mysterious in the bottle. Jäger itself is a 35% ABV herbal liqueur, about the same strength as many flavored spirits and a bit weaker than standard vodka or whiskey. What makes the next morning so rough is *how* people usually drink it: as ice-cold shots, often several in a row, often dropped into an energy drink as a Jägerbomb, and often late in a night that already involved plenty of alcohol. Fast shots push your blood alcohol up quickly, the sugar and cold hide how strong it is, and the caffeine in a Jägerbomb can keep you drinking and keep you awake long after your body wanted to stop. This guide breaks down each of those pieces, separates the myths from the real causes, and covers what actually helps.

**The quick rules:** Treat a Jäger shot as a full standard drink, because it roughly is one. Space shots out instead of lining them up. If you drink Jägerbombs, cap the number and stop at least a few hours before bed so the caffeine has a chance to wear off. Drink water between rounds and eat a real meal beforehand. If you are already hungover, rehydrate, eat something gentle, and rest.

> **When to get help, not just ride it out.** A hangover is miserable but passes on its own, usually within a day. Rounds of fast shots are also one of the classic routes to **alcohol poisoning**, which is a medical emergency. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or long pauses), has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Don't leave them to "sleep it off" alone, and roll them onto their side if they are vomiting. **See a doctor soon if** you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, notice blood in vomit or stool, have chest pain or a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, or feel worse rather than better after 24 hours. If you find yourself getting shaky, sweaty or anxious every time you stop drinking after a run of heavy days, that is worth raising with a doctor, too. It is a physical signal, not a character flaw, and it is very treatable.

## What Is Actually in Jägermeister?

Jägermeister is a German herbal liqueur first developed in 1934 in Wolfenbüttel, Lower Saxony. The company says the recipe uses 56 herbs, blossoms, roots and fruits, and the full list is a closely guarded secret. Ingredients that have been widely reported over the years include citrus peel, licorice, anise, ginger, juniper, saffron and ginseng, though the company does not publish exact amounts.

Here is what matters for a hangover:

| Feature | What it means for the next morning |
|---|---|
| **Alcohol strength: 35% ABV (70 proof)** in most markets | Lower than 40% vodka or whiskey, but a standard shot still holds close to a full standard drink of alcohol. |
| **It's a liqueur, so it's sweetened** | The sugar and herbal flavor soften the burn, which makes it easy to drink more and faster than you would with a straight spirit. |
| **Dark color and botanical extracts** | Jäger is not a "clean" neutral spirit like vodka. It carries plant compounds and coloring, though there is no published data on its exact congener levels. |
| **Usually served ice cold** | Cold dulls the taste of both sugar and alcohol, so it goes down with less warning. |

### Debunking the classic Jäger myths

A few rumors have followed Jägermeister around for decades. None of them explain your hangover.

- **"It contains deer blood."** It doesn't. The deer on the label comes from the legend of Saint Hubertus, the patron saint of hunters. "Jägermeister" roughly means "master hunter" in German. There is no animal product in it.
- **"It contains opium or something illegal."** No. This one probably comes from poppy seeds being rumored as one of the herbs. Poppy seeds used in food and drink don't make a drink a narcotic, and Jäger is sold legally around the world as an ordinary liqueur.
- **"The herbs give it a special kind of drunk."** There's no good evidence for this. The effects of Jägermeister come from its alcohol, plus the caffeine if you mix it with an energy drink. The herbs are there for flavor.

## Why Jägermeister Hangovers Feel So Bad

A hangover comes from several things happening at once: your body breaking down alcohol into a toxic intermediate called acetaldehyde, mild dehydration, disrupted sleep, an irritated stomach, low blood sugar, and an inflammatory response from your immune system. Researchers still argue about how much each piece contributes, but they agree on one thing: **the amount of alcohol you drink, and how fast you drink it, matters more than anything else.**

Jäger nights tend to hit almost every one of those triggers hard. Here are the five main reasons.

### 1. Shots raise your blood alcohol fast

Sipping a cocktail over 30 minutes and knocking back a shot in two seconds deliver alcohol to your body very differently. A shot lands in your stomach all at once and moves into your bloodstream quickly, especially if you haven't eaten. Your liver can only process roughly one standard drink an hour, no matter how quickly it arrives. When you stack several shots in a short window, your blood alcohol climbs well past what your liver can keep up with, and the backlog keeps you drunk, and then hungover, for longer.

This is also why Jäger often appears at the worst point in the night. It tends to be a "round for the table" drink, ordered after people have already had a few. A round or two of shots on top of an evening of beer or wine can easily be the difference between a rough morning and a lost day.

### 2. Sugar and cold make it easy to drink more

Jägermeister is sweet. The company doesn't put a sugar figure on US bottles, but it is a liqueur, which means sugar is part of the recipe, and it tastes noticeably sweeter than a straight spirit. Serving it close to freezing numbs your taste buds even further.

Sugar itself is probably not a major cause of hangovers. There's no good evidence that a sweet drink, by itself, makes the next morning worse than the same amount of alcohol in an unsweetened drink. The real problem is behavioral: when a drink doesn't taste strong, people drink it faster and in greater quantity. Sweet, cold shots hide how much alcohol you've had until it catches up with you.

There is one more small effect worth knowing. Alcohol interferes with your liver's ability to release stored glucose, which is part of why people often feel shaky, weak and foggy the next morning. A burst of sugar from sweet drinks doesn't protect you from that dip, and sugary mixers can leave you craving more sugar the next day without fixing anything.

### 3. Herbal congeners, maybe

Congeners are the chemical by-products and flavor compounds that come along with alcohol, especially in darker drinks. A well-known study from researchers at Brown University (Rohsenow and colleagues, 2010) gave volunteers either bourbon or vodka to the same blood alcohol level and found the bourbon, which is much higher in congeners, produced somewhat worse hangovers on average. The difference was real but modest. The amount of alcohol still mattered far more than the type.

Jägermeister is dark, herbal and full of plant extracts, so it is reasonable to guess it sits closer to the "darker drink" end of that scale than vodka does. But that's an informed guess, not a measured fact. There is no published research measuring Jägermeister's congener levels or testing Jäger hangovers specifically. If you notice Jäger hits you harder than the same amount of vodka, congeners might play a small part, but the shot-taking pattern is almost certainly the bigger factor. For more background on this, see our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### 4. Jägerbombs add caffeine and a lot more sugar

The Jägerbomb (a shot of Jäger dropped into a glass of energy drink, usually Red Bull) is where most of the legendary Jäger hangovers come from. We cover it in detail in the next section.

### 5. Jäger nights wreck your sleep

Alcohol already makes sleep worse. It can help you drift off, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep, the deep dreaming stage your brain needs to feel rested. Add caffeine from energy drinks, a late finish, and maybe a loud bar, and you can wake up having had very little real sleep. Poor sleep alone makes people feel foggy, irritable and achy, and it makes every other hangover symptom feel worse.

## Jägerbomb Hangovers: Why the Energy Drink Makes It Worse

A Jägerbomb combines a shot of Jäger with a measure of energy drink. A standard 8.4 oz (250 ml) can of Red Bull contains 80 mg of caffeine and 27 grams of sugar, according to the label. Bars often split a can between two or three drinks, but over a few rounds the caffeine and sugar add up quickly.

### "Wide awake drunk"

Caffeine does not sober you up. It doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, and it doesn't lower your blood alcohol. What it does is make you *feel* less drunk. Researchers sometimes call this "wide awake drunkenness." Lab studies, including a 2006 study by Ferreira and colleagues in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, found that people who mixed alcohol with an energy drink reported feeling less impaired, even though objective tests of their coordination and reaction time showed they were just as impaired as people who drank alcohol alone.

That gap between how drunk you feel and how drunk you are is the core problem. The normal signals that tell you to slow down or go home (sleepiness, heaviness, feeling sloppy) get muffled. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that people who mix alcohol with energy drinks are more likely to binge drink than people who don't. In 2010, the FDA also warned several makers of pre-mixed caffeinated alcoholic drinks that the added caffeine was an unsafe additive, which is why those canned products were reformulated.

### What that means for the morning

The energy drink itself does not cause a hangover in the way alcohol does. In fact, research on caffeine's direct effect on hangover severity is mixed, and it does not appear to change much on its own. The damage is mostly indirect:

- **You drink more.** Feeling more awake makes it easier to keep going, and more alcohol is the single biggest driver of a worse hangover.
- **You sleep less and worse.** Caffeine lasts for hours in your body. Several Jägerbombs late at night can keep you lying awake or sleeping lightly even after the alcohol has started to wear off. If this is a familiar pattern, see our piece on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).
- **Your heart works harder.** Alcohol and caffeine both can raise your heart rate. Some people notice a pounding or racing heart late at night or the next morning. If that happens to you, our guide on a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains what's normal and what isn't.
- **Your stomach gets hit twice.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and carbonated, acidic, sugary mixers can add to the discomfort. That's part of why Jägerbomb nights often end in nausea.

**A sensible rule:** if you drink Jägerbombs at all, keep it to one or two, treat each one as a full drink plus a coffee, and stop several hours before you plan to sleep.

## Is a Jäger Hangover Worse Than Other Drinks?

Ounce for ounce of alcohol, there's no good evidence that Jägermeister causes worse hangovers than other spirits. The research we do have points to the same thing over and over: **total alcohol and drinking speed matter most, and darker drinks may add a little on top.**

Here's a practical comparison:

| Drink | Typical alcohol | Hangover factors |
|---|---|---|
| **Jäger shot (straight)** | 35% ABV | Fast intake, sweet and cold so easy to overdo, herbal compounds of unknown effect |
| **Jägerbomb** | 35% ABV shot plus energy drink | All of the above, plus caffeine that masks drunkenness and hurts sleep, plus extra sugar |
| **Vodka soda** | 40% ABV spirit, diluted | Low in congeners, usually sipped, less sugar |
| **Whiskey or bourbon** | 40% ABV or more | Higher congeners, often sipped, though shots are common too |
| **Tequila shots** | 40% ABV | Fast intake is the main issue, as with Jäger |

If you want to compare, see our guides on the [vodka hangover](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), the [whiskey hangover](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), and the [truth about tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth). The common thread in all of them is the same: shots and speed make every drink worse.

### What about mixing Jäger with beer or wine?

You've probably heard "beer before liquor, never been sicker." A 2019 randomized study published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* tested this directly and found that the order you drink beer and wine in made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. What mattered was how much people drank in total and how drunk they felt. So the problem with ending a beer night on Jäger shots isn't the order. It's that the shots add a lot of extra alcohol on top. More on that in our [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) breakdown.

## Common Jäger Hangover Symptoms

Most people describe a Jäger hangover the same way any heavy hangover feels, often with a few extras from the energy drink:

- **Pounding headache.** From alcohol's effects on blood vessels, dehydration, poor sleep and inflammation. Our guide to the [alcohol headache](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) covers the causes in more depth.
- **Nausea and an upset stomach.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and slows how it empties. Sweet, fizzy mixers don't help. See our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) for what settles it.
- **Shaky, weak, foggy feeling.** Partly from low blood sugar, partly from poor sleep, partly from your nervous system rebounding after alcohol's sedating effect.
- **Jittery or anxious feeling.** More common after Jägerbombs, when caffeine and the alcohol rebound overlap.
- **Exhaustion.** Short, broken sleep is common after a night of shots.
- **Thirst and dry mouth.** Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water.

## How to Prevent a Jäger Hangover

The only guaranteed way to avoid a hangover is not to drink, or to drink very little. If you are going to drink Jäger, these habits make the biggest difference, roughly in order of impact.

### Before you go out

- **Eat a real meal.** Food in your stomach, especially protein, fat and fiber, slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Shots on an empty stomach are the fastest route to a high blood alcohol level.
- **Decide on a number.** Shots are easy to lose count of, especially as part of a group round. Picking a limit ahead of time is more effective than deciding in the moment.

### While you're drinking

- **Count each shot as a standard drink.** A 1.5 oz pour of a 35% liqueur holds slightly more than half an ounce of pure alcohol, which is close to a US standard drink. Two Jäger shots is roughly the same alcohol as two beers, just much faster.
- **Space your shots.** Leave at least an hour between them where you can. Your liver can't speed up to match you.
- **Drink water between rounds.** A glass of water per drink slows your pace and helps with dehydration. It won't stop a hangover if you drink a lot, but it helps.
- **Skip the Jägerbomb, or cap it at one or two.** If you want the taste, have Jäger on its own and sip it chilled rather than as a bomb.
- **Make Jäger the only shot of the night.** Mixing many types of shots isn't harmful because of the mix itself, but it usually means more total alcohol.

### Before bed

- **Stop drinking a few hours before you sleep** if you can, especially if you've had caffeine.
- **Drink a large glass of water and eat a small snack.** Something with carbohydrates can help with the morning blood sugar dip.
- **Lay out water and something simple for the morning.**

For a fuller set of evidence-based habits, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## How to Recover From a Jäger Hangover

There's no fast cure. Your body needs time to finish clearing alcohol and its by-products, rebalance fluids and catch up on sleep. You can make the wait easier.

1. **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water over the morning rather than chugging it. If you've been vomiting or sweating a lot, an oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix can help. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains when they're worth it.
2. **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, rice or broth are easy on the stomach and help bring your blood sugar back up.
3. **Go easy on more caffeine.** One normal coffee is fine if you drink it daily, because skipping it can add a withdrawal headache. But stacking more caffeine on top of a Jägerbomb night can make jitters and a racing heart worse.
4. **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen can help a headache but can irritate an already upset stomach, so take it with food. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is harder on the liver after heavy drinking. Our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the risks. Stick to the label dose either way.
5. **Rest.** Sleep is the most underrated hangover treatment. A nap does more than most remedies.
6. **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another drink may delay symptoms briefly, but it just pushes the hangover later and adds more alcohol for your body to deal with.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honest Version)

Some people who drink occasionally add a supplement to their routine. One of the most studied is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree.

Here's an honest summary of the evidence. Most of the research on DHM comes from lab and animal studies, which suggest it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde and may reduce some of alcohol's effects on the brain. Human data is still limited, with only small studies. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers from heavy drinking. It certainly doesn't make rounds of shots or Jägerbombs safe, and it does nothing about the caffeine side of a Jägerbomb.

If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands side by side. If you take any prescription medicine, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Jägermeister is a 35% ABV herbal liqueur. It isn't stronger than most spirits, and there's no special ingredient that makes its hangovers worse.
- The rough mornings come from **how it's drunk**: fast, cold, sweet shots that add a lot of alcohol in a short time, often late in a night.
- **Jägerbombs** add caffeine that hides how drunk you are and hurts your sleep, plus extra sugar. They tend to lead to drinking more.
- Herbal congeners may play a small role, but nobody has measured that for Jäger specifically.
- The fixes are simple: eat first, count every shot as a full drink, space them out, drink water, cap or skip the Jägerbombs, and stop well before bed.
- Know the signs of alcohol poisoning. If someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or is vomiting while barely conscious, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does Jägermeister give me such a bad hangover?**

Mostly because of how it's usually drunk. Jäger is almost always taken as fast, ice-cold shots, often several in a row and often late in a night of drinking, which raises your blood alcohol quickly. It's sweet and cold, so it's easy to drink more than you realize. If you drink it as a Jägerbomb, the energy drink's caffeine can make you feel less drunk and keep you drinking longer, then disrupt your sleep. Its herbal compounds may add a little, but that hasn't been studied directly.

**Are Jägerbombs worse for hangovers than plain Jäger?**

Usually, yes, but mostly indirectly. Caffeine doesn't lower your blood alcohol or speed up how fast you clear it, but it makes you feel less impaired, which tends to lead to drinking more. Research also shows that people who mix alcohol with energy drinks are more likely to binge. On top of that, the caffeine can keep you awake or sleeping lightly, and poor sleep makes a hangover feel worse. If you drink them, keep it to one or two and stop several hours before bed.

**How much alcohol is in a shot of Jägermeister?**

Jägermeister is 35% alcohol by volume (70 proof) in most markets. A standard 1.5 oz (44 ml) shot holds a little over half an ounce of pure alcohol, which is close to one US standard drink. That means two Jäger shots is roughly the same alcohol as two regular beers, just taken in seconds instead of over an hour.

**Does the sugar in Jägermeister cause hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that sugar itself is a major cause of hangovers. The problem with sweet drinks is that they hide the taste of alcohol, so people drink them faster and in larger amounts. Jägerbombs add a lot more sugar from the energy drink, which doesn't help an upset stomach. The alcohol is still the main driver.

**Is Jägermeister worse than vodka for hangovers?**

For the same amount of alcohol, probably only slightly, if at all. Research comparing bourbon with vodka found that the darker, higher-congener drink caused somewhat worse hangovers on average, and Jäger is a dark herbal liqueur, so it may sit closer to that end. But no study has tested Jäger directly, and the difference in the bourbon study was modest. How much and how fast you drink matters far more than which bottle it came from.

**Does Jägermeister really contain deer blood?**

No. That's a long-running myth. The deer on the label refers to the legend of Saint Hubertus, the patron saint of hunters, and the name roughly means "master hunter" in German. Jägermeister is made from herbs, roots, fruits and spices, alcohol, sugar and water. It contains no animal products.

**How long does a Jägermeister hangover last?**

Most hangovers ease within about 24 hours, with the worst symptoms in the morning and early afternoon. After a heavy night of shots or Jägerbombs, it can take most of the next day to feel normal, especially if you slept badly. If you feel worse rather than better after 24 hours, can't keep fluids down, or have chest pain or a heartbeat that won't settle, see a doctor.

**Can DHM help with a Jägermeister hangover?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers from heavy drinking, and it won't do anything about the caffeine in Jägerbombs. Lab and animal research suggests it may support alcohol metabolism, and some people include it in their routine, but human studies are small. The habits that make the biggest difference are eating first, pacing your shots, drinking water, and limiting the total number of drinks.
